video.title: This Kid Found the Fastest Way to Make Money With AI Apps

summary: The video is an interview with George, a young founder who built mobile apps using an AI app builder despite having no coding experience. His wrestling app, Wrestle AI, grew through creator partnerships and subscriptions, while newer boxing and workout apps used creator content and Meta ads. He also describes earlier experiments, including Fight AI, a supplement brand, dropshipping, and a failed reaction app. The main takeaway is to pair a clear, easy-to-demo feature with the right audience, then measure whether customers stay and pay rather than relying on views alone.

ideas.name: Fight AI
ideas.one_liner: A mobile app that analyzes videos of MMA training or matches and suggests ways to improve.
ideas.customer: MMA and other fight-sport athletes who want feedback on training or match videos.
ideas.problem: Athletes want feedback on their form, strengths, weaknesses, and ways to improve.
ideas.offer: Upload a video of a match, training, or shadow boxing for an AI breakdown. The app was built first as a test for George and then launched as a broader fight-sport app.

pricing.notes: The transcript does not say whether these prices are still current.

acquisition_channels.details: George and a friend posted videos on a new Instagram account; later, they sponsored meme pages, including one creator with a strong following in the niche.

quote.text: We just posted about it. Like just post a few dumb videos on just your friends.
quote.speaker: George

acquisition_channels.details: They sponsored meme pages and a creator whose audience reacted strongly to sponsorship posts.

ideas.delivery: The customer uploads a video in the mobile app and receives an AI-generated breakdown. George built the app with an AI app builder; the transcript does not describe ongoing support or review of analyses.
unit_economics_claims: The app generated about $500 in monthly recurring revenue after launch, according to George.
George said it made about $1,800 in its first month.
George later said it still makes over $1,000 per month without active maintenance.
George estimated monthly churn at about 30%.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. George said he built it himself with an AI app builder.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Revenue arrived in the first month; exact time to the first sale was not stated.

acquisition.how: Organic posts and paid promotion can be scheduled or optimized with software, but creator selection and sponsorship coordination require human judgment. Unsolicited DMs to individual creators may not be lawful in the UK without consent.

onboarding.how: The app can guide users through upload and subscription onboarding, with occasional human review for confusing cases.

delivery.how: Video analysis and feedback are software-delivered; a human may still need to review inaccurate or unsafe advice.

billing.how: Subscription billing can run through an app store with occasional refund or payment exceptions.

support.how: Routine support could be handled with automated help, but video-analysis complaints and sport-specific questions may need a knowledgeable person.

uk_applicability.notes: A mobile training-feedback app can serve UK users much as it serves US users. App-store rules, privacy, and consumer subscription requirements still apply.

risks: George said the app's initial growth later fizzled and that it was not actively maintained.
The app may have limited repeat use if customers run out of useful videos to analyze.
AI feedback may miss sport-specific details or give unhelpful technique advice.

ideas.name: Wrestle AI
ideas.one_liner: A subscription app for wrestlers that analyzes technique videos and adds training, weight-management, and practice features.
ideas.business_model: Subscription app; George and his wrestling-influencer partner split the business 50/50.
ideas.customer: Wrestlers, including high-school and college athletes and younger wrestlers; some features support training without a coach.
ideas.problem: Wrestlers need accessible technique feedback and tools to support practice and weight management.
ideas.offer: The app analyzes uploaded wrestling videos for fundamentals and technique. Other features include calorie tracking, a wrestling calendar, weight tracking, stance-in-motion drills, and practice mode.

pricing.model: Monthly or annual subscription, with the trial attached to the annual plan and an exit offer for some users.
pricing.notes: George said most users chose the annual plan because the trial was attached to it. An abandoned-yearly offer could show a discount after a user tapped to exit.

acquisition_channels.details: George partnered with a wrestling creator, then paid niche creators per video or on CPM deals. He tracked creators and scaled the ones that brought useful customers.

quote.text: And from there we started just sponsoring a bunch of different creators.
quote.speaker: George

acquisition_channels.details: The partner and other creators posted videos about the app; George also used creator posts as candidates for paid ads.
They later tested paid social, initially optimizing for installs and later learning to optimize campaigns for purchases.

quote.text: But if you want like like to make your ads 10 times more profitable, you optimize for purchases.
quote.speaker: George

ideas.delivery: Users receive automated app analysis and digital tools. George built the app and product systems with an AI app builder; his partner supplied a wrestling audience and promotion. A VA helped find creators, and George described building an internal tool to track the business.
unit_economics_claims: The app made about $8,000 in its first week and about $17,000 in its first month, according to George.
George said the second month was about $19,000, December was about $30,000, and January was about $40,000.
George reported about $28,000 in February, $20,000 in March, $15,000 in April, and a current floor of about $10,000.
George said the most expensive month for tokens was about $2,000.
George estimated a first purchase averaged about $25, with roughly half choosing the annual plan and half the monthly plan.
George estimated a $1,000 influencer spend at a $2 CPM could return about $2,500 to $5,000 in revenue.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. George said Apple-held revenue left him with about $1,000 in the bank to sustain growth during one period.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: The first week after launch; George said the app made about $8,000 in that week.

acquisition.how: Paid ads and creator content can be managed with software, but choosing creators and negotiating deals required George's judgment. UK outreach by unsolicited DM to individual creators may breach PECR without consent.

onboarding.how: App onboarding, trials, and subscription choices can be automated, subject to clear pricing and compliant consent flows.

delivery.how: Video analysis, calorie tracking, calendar parsing, and practice prompts are software-delivered. Human review may be needed for inaccurate technique or weight guidance.

billing.how: App subscriptions and annual trials can be billed automatically, with human handling for refunds, disputes, and app-store issues.

support.how: Common app questions can be automated, but sport-specific advice, account problems, and safety-sensitive weight questions may need human support.

uk_applicability.notes: Wrestling and app subscriptions translate to the UK. The product would need UK-compliant privacy, subscription disclosures, and careful handling of calorie and weight-management advice.

risks: Demand is seasonal and tied to wrestling season; George said he planned to coast and rebuild the product out of season.
The video-analysis feature may become less useful after a wrestler has repeated the same fundamentals or run out of matches to analyze.
Weight-management advice can create safety and regulatory concerns, especially for young athletes.
George described a competitor threatening legal action, though he said they did not sue.
George said Apple removed a newer app for two weeks after a public paywall dispute, illustrating app-store review and reputation risk.

ideas.name: Boxing opponent-analysis app
ideas.one_liner: An app that analyzes an opponent's video to identify patterns a boxer can use in a fight.
ideas.business_model: App revenue with paid social user acquisition; exact subscription terms are not stated.
ideas.customer: Boxers and fight-sport athletes preparing for an opponent.
ideas.problem: A fighter may miss repeatable patterns in an opponent's movements and openings.
ideas.offer: The app analyzes an opponent's video, such as identifying that the opponent drops their hands after a specific exchange.

acquisition_channels.details: The team used creator-made ads and Meta ads, with the product demonstrated early in short videos.

quote.text: And then I started like learning how the meta ads algorithm worked.
quote.speaker: George

acquisition_channels.details: Creators made short demonstration videos; some were posted organically and some were used as paid ads.

ideas.delivery: A user uploads an opponent's video and receives software-generated analysis. A trusted collaborator makes or edits ad videos, while George directs and funds the project.
unit_economics_claims: George said the boxing app spent about $400 per day and returned about $900 to $1,200 on day one.
George described day-one return as roughly 2x to 4x ad spend, with higher lifetime return expected.
George said the app had generated about $23,000 lifetime revenue.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. George said he was funding the project himself.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: George said the two newer apps reached about $10,000 within 45 days; the specific first-sale time was not stated.

acquisition.how: Meta ad delivery and creator ad testing can be automated substantially, with human review of creative and spend. Unsolicited creator DMs in the UK may be restricted by PECR.

onboarding.how: A mobile app can automate account creation, video upload guidance, and subscription onboarding.

delivery.how: AI video analysis is software-delivered; a human should review performance and handle inaccurate or strategically consequential advice.

billing.how: Subscription payments can be automated through an app payment provider, with occasional refunds and disputes needing review.

support.how: Automated help can handle routine app questions, while analysis quality and account issues may need human support.

uk_applicability.notes: The use case can serve UK boxing users. Privacy and rights to uploaded footage, plus UK consumer subscription rules, need to be addressed.

risks: The transcript gives limited evidence about retention, customer acquisition cost over the full customer lifetime, or the reliability of the analysis.
Users may upload footage they do not have permission to use.
Ad performance can change as audiences and creatives fatigue.

ideas.name: Abs-analysis workout app
ideas.one_liner: A fitness app that rates a user's abs from a photo and suggests workouts to improve them.
ideas.business_model: App subscriptions with paid social acquisition; exact price is not stated.
ideas.customer: People seeking a more defined six-pack.
ideas.problem: Generic fitness apps may feel broad; users want a specific assessment and workout plan for their abs.
ideas.offer: The user takes a photo of their abs, receives a rating, and can see tailored workouts. George said ads worked better when they showed the rating and the workout rather than just the score.

pricing.model: Subscription app; exact pricing is not stated.
pricing.notes: George discussed a paywall listing monthly and weekly terms, but the transcript does not clearly establish whether this was the same app.

acquisition_channels.details: The team tested Meta ads, learning that creative showing a workout tailored to the user's abs performed better for retention than a rating-only creative.

quote.text: the best type of videos were the ones that would show the actual it would be rating workout and then them doing the workout.
quote.speaker: George

acquisition_channels.details: They initially sponsored creators, but George said the early creator choices did not produce strong results.

ideas.delivery: The customer uploads a photo and receives an AI rating and workout guidance through the app. The transcript does not state who provides ongoing support or reviews results.
unit_economics_claims: George said the workout app had generated about $15,000 lifetime revenue and about $8,000 in the current month.
George said a co-founder reported a download-to-paid conversion rate above 20%; George cited about 5% as an average.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; George said the newer apps reached about $10,000 within 45 days.

acquisition.how: Paid social can automate targeting and delivery, while creative testing and budget decisions still need human oversight.

onboarding.how: Photo upload, onboarding, and subscription prompts can run in the app, with checks that pricing is clear and compliant.

delivery.how: Image assessment and workout suggestions can be delivered by software, but fitness and body-image advice needs quality controls.

billing.how: App subscriptions can be billed automatically; refunds, disputes, and paywall compliance need review.

support.how: Automated support can answer routine questions, while sensitive body-image or exercise-safety concerns may need a person.

uk_applicability.notes: The app concept can serve UK customers, subject to privacy, consumer subscription rules, and careful presentation of body-image and fitness claims.

risks: George said rating-only ads attracted downloads but users churned quickly.
A high download-to-paid conversion rate does not establish long-term retention or customer satisfaction.
George said a public post about the paywall preceded a two-week removal from the app store; the exact reason was disputed.

tactics.name: Find niche creators using average views
steps: Use a VA to review the creator feed in the target niche.
Shortlist creators averaging more than 25,000 views per video, rather than sorting by follower count.
Send a clear paid-promotion proposal and track replies, views, and resulting sales.
In the UK, do not send unsolicited marketing DMs to individual creators without the required consent; use consent-based introductions or lawful channels.

quote.text: scroll on my for you page and outreach to everyone who has over 25,000 views on average.
quote.speaker: George

tactics.name: Use a VA for creator sourcing
steps: After the first $1,000 in revenue, George recommends hiring a virtual assistant.
He sourced VAs through Fiverr or Upwork.
Show the VA the target niche, the creator feed to inspect, the view threshold, and the message script.

quote.text: After you make your first thousand bucks, hire a VA instantly.
quote.speaker: George

tactics.name: Use a short creator brief and test deal structures
steps: State that the message is a paid promotion in its opening words.
Explain the app briefly and say why the creator's content is a fit.
Test flat-fee and CPM deals, then compare the results against attributable sales.
Keep proven creators and stop spending on creators who do not produce engagement or sales.

quote.text: The DM should be paid promo and the paid promo for app name. That should be the first line.
quote.speaker: George

tactics.name: Choose creators by content skill and audience fit
steps: Compare creators' average views and audience fit, not just their follower totals or athletic reputation.
Watch comments and engagement to judge whether the audience understands the product.
Start with a small test; retain creators whose content drives useful outcomes.

quote.text: the ROI on like a a really good wrestler that's not that good at content Yeah. isn't really as big as the ROI on even though they have so much accolades.
quote.speaker: George

tactics.name: Turn successful organic creator videos into paid ads
steps: Find organic creator videos that demonstrate the product clearly.
Ask the creator to make a separate ad video when the organic integration is too subtle for paid placements.
Show the app and its result early; George advised putting the product in the first 15 seconds.
Study competing ads in Meta Ads Library and test creatives on Meta placements.

quote.text: you need to show the product within the first 15 seconds
quote.speaker: George

tactics.name: Lead with one clear product feature
steps: Choose one visually clear feature that explains the app quickly.
Use that feature to bring users into the app, even if other features drive repeat use.
When one feature's content becomes familiar, introduce another useful feature to renew attention.

quote.text: understand your app needs a gotcha feature, right? It needs one feature that you run advertising on.
quote.speaker: George

tactics.name: Measure customer quality, not just views or downloads
steps: Track paid conversion, repeat use, churn, and sales alongside social views.
Compare creatives that generate downloads with creatives that demonstrate how the product helps.
Stop treating a large view count as success when users do not stay or pay.

quote.text: Both apps got a million views in its first month. Wrestle AI the first month did 17K. Green did $35.
quote.speaker: George

tactics.name: Make annual plans support growth, but consider monthly plans when growth is not the priority
steps: George attached the trial to the annual subscription, encouraging customers to commit to a year.
He preferred front-loaded annual revenue while aggressively funding growth.
He suggested monthly plans may suit a business that is not trying to grow as quickly.

quote.text: I would always try to frontload revenue this way I had more for your growth
quote.speaker: George

tactics.name: Optimize ad campaigns for purchases
steps: Track purchases rather than only app installs.
Use a purchase event for campaign optimization when the app and tracking setup support it.
Compare cost per purchase and downstream revenue before increasing spend.

quote.text: But if you want like like to make your ads 10 times more profitable, you optimize for purchases.
quote.speaker: George

tactics.name: Use first creator deals to build credibility and referrals
steps: Run a manageable first creator test and review comments, views, and sales.
Use successful collaborations as social proof when approaching other creators.
Make the creator relationship and the product's fit clear rather than assuming a large audience alone will convert.

quote.text: even on your first it's okay to be unprofitable on your first few influencers because they're going to start spreading your word to other influencers.
quote.speaker: George

tactics.name: Keep campaign and business data in one place
steps: Track creator deals, contracts, ad metrics, and business results in an internal dashboard.
Connect the relevant data sources so the operator can ask consistent questions about daily results and profit and loss.
Use the data to make decisions, then check attribution against actual performance.

quote.text: It tracks I run my entire business on it. my my metads, my creators, like literally dashboard contracts are sent through it.

tactics.name: Treat app-store and platform relationships carefully
steps: Make subscription options and terms clear in the paywall.
Avoid public claims about borderline compliance that could attract review or enforcement.
If an account or listing is restricted, appeal through the platform and document the issue rather than assuming the first decision is final.

quote.text: if you're doing anything that's anything close to being gray, never do that on Twitter cuz Apple's on there like a hawk.

tactics.name: Protect runway and set a growth budget
steps: Keep enough operating cash available to continue growth while platform payouts are delayed.
Decide how much cash can be invested in ads without putting personal runway at risk.
George said he was more willing to scale once he had money set aside for living costs.

tactics.name: Test a product's core feature before expanding the feature set
steps: Build the feature that makes the product easy to explain and test whether the audience wants it.
Use repeated customer behavior to identify where the first feature stops being useful.
Add adjacent features that solve repeat-use problems, such as Wrestle AI's calorie and weight-management tools.

warnings.warning: Unsolicited marketing DMs to individual creators may be restricted by UK PECR; the interview's US-based outreach playbook should not be copied into the UK without a lawful basis and appropriate consent.

The host and guest described an app-store pricing presentation that drew scrutiny. Subscription prices, trial terms, and billing intervals should be presented clearly and in the order required by platform rules.
Weight-cutting and calorie-tracking features aimed at young wrestlers can create health and safety risks; the transcript does not describe qualified clinical oversight.
Creator view counts can be manipulated; George said he checked comment quality and engagement, but also acknowledged that much of the sales attribution was intuition.
George described a competitor threatening to sue and discussing an NDA. He chose not to sign an agreement he did not understand.

evidence_quality.rationale: George describes his own apps, creator acquisition process, product features, and revenue with substantial detail. The numbers are self-reported, several are approximate, some timelines and app revenue figures are inconsistent, and no independent records are shown.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host included a sponsored GoHighLevel advertisement and promoted his Playmakers AI agency program and paid business-plan membership. Those sponsor and promotional segments were excluded as business ideas.
